title: get
subtitle: get a job / get hungry / get to work
summary: Use get with a noun (= receive, buy, find), with an adjective (= become), and with to / in / out / on / off to talk about arriving and travelling.

lesson.heading: get + noun = receive, buy, find
lesson.text: First you don't have something. Then you **get** it. Now you have it. So **get** + a noun can mean receive, buy or find.

examples.text: *A:* Did you **get** my postcard? *B:* Yes, I **got** it yesterday.
I like your sweater. Where did you **get** it?
Is it difficult to **get** a job at the moment?
*A:* Hello, can I speak to Lisa, please? *B:* Sure. I'll **get** her.

lesson.heading: get a bus / a train / a taxi
lesson.text: We also say **get a bus**, **get a train** and **get a taxi**. Here **get** means take.

examples.text: *A:* Did you walk here? *B:* No, I **got** the bus.
I don't want to walk home. Let's **get** a taxi.

lesson.heading: get + adjective = become
lesson.text: First you're not hungry. Then you **get** hungry. Now you are hungry. So **get** + an adjective means become.

examples.text: If you don't eat, you **get hungry**.
Drink your coffee. It**'s getting cold**.
I'm sorry your mother is ill. I hope she **gets better** soon.
It was raining very hard. We didn't have an umbrella, so we **got** very **wet**.

lesson.heading: get married / get dressed / get lost
lesson.text: Some very common phrases work in the same way. **get dressed** = put your clothes on. **get lost** = lose your way.

examples.text: Nicole and Frank are **getting married** soon.
I got up and **got dressed** quickly.
We didn't have a map, so we **got lost**.

lesson.heading: get to a place = arrive
lesson.text: **get to** a place means arrive there. But we say **get here**, **get there** and **get home** with no *to*.

examples.text: We left London at 10 o'clock and **got to Manchester** at 12.45.
How did you **get here**? By bus?
What time did you **get home** last night?

lesson.heading: get in / out / on / off
rows: Kate **got in the car** and drove away.
A car stopped and a man **got out**.
get on (a bus / a train / a plane)
you go on to a bus, train or plane
We **got on the bus** outside the hotel.
get off (a bus / a train / a plane)
you leave a bus, train or plane
lesson.note: You can also say *Kate got into the car* and *A man got out of the car*.

lesson.text: We travel *in* a car but *on* a bus, so we **get in** a car and **get on** a bus.

exercises.prompt: Where did you ___? It's very nice.
exercises.explanation: Here get = buy: Where did you get your jacket?

exercises.prompt: Quick! This man is ill. We must ___.
exercises.explanation: Here get = find or bring: We must get a doctor.
After it's we need the -ing form: It's getting dark (= it is becoming dark).

exercises.prompt: *A:* Where's Karen? *B:* She's ___ to go out.
exercises.explanation: get + adjective: she is becoming ready.

exercises.prompt: Don't go out in the rain. You'll ___.
exercises.explanation: get + adjective = become: you'll get wet.

exercises.prompt: Martin is always very calm. He never ___.
exercises.explanation: After he we use gets: he never gets angry.

exercises.prompt: Does get mean receive/buy/find here, or does it mean become?
Match the two halves of each sentence.

pairs.left: We tried to find the hotel, but
Everybody wants to stay young, but
The weather is horrible here in winter.
pairs.right: We get a lot of rain.

pairs.left: Margaret has got a well-paid job.

pairs.right: I hope he gets the job.

pairs.left: My brother got married last year.

exercises.prompt: Yesterday the weather wasn't so good at first, but it ___ during the day.
exercises.explanation: The past of get is got: the weather got better.

exercises.prompt: I ___ the bus and walked to my house from the bus stop.
exercises.hint: (got in / got out of / got on / got off)
exercises.explanation: We get on a bus and we get off a bus.

exercises.statement: I made a stupid mistake. I got in the wrong train.
exercises.explanation: I got on the wrong train. We use get on and get off with a bus, a train or a plane.

exercises.prompt: Somebody left home at 7.30 and arrived at work at 8.15. Put the sentence in order.
exercises.answer: I left home at 7.30 and got to work at 8.15.
exercises.explanation: get to a place = arrive there.
